entry.title: Managing Inactive Contacts in Email Marketing: Balancing Deliverability Risk with List Value
entry.content:
Why Inactive Contacts Carry Both Value and Risk

Inactive contacts — subscribers on a mailing list who have not recently opened, clicked, or converted — are a normal part of every email marketing programme. They carry both value and risk.

The value: sending to inactive contacts performs a discovery function, identifying contacts who are naturally returning to a buying phase. Excluding them entirely makes it harder to build brand awareness, retain customers, and identify signals that indicate where a contact is in the customer lifecycle.

The risk: mismanaging inactive contacts — sending too frequently, sending irrelevant content, or failing to remove contacts who have been inactive for too long — damages sender reputation and causes deliverability issues, including blocked emails, bounced messages, and loss of inbox placement.

The goal is not to eliminate inactive contacts from the programme but to manage them in a way that captures their value while controlling the risk they introduce. This article explains both how to measure the health of that balance using proactive metrics, and how to act on those metrics through data management and targeting strategy.

Why Inactive Contacts Are a Normal and Valuable Part of Email Marketing

After a full-list send — an email sent to the entire mailing list rather than a targeted segment — the majority of opens, clicks, and conversions will come from the most active contacts. This is expected. However, a proportion of engagement and revenue will also come from contacts who were classified as inactive before that campaign.

This happens because sending to the full list performs a discovery function: it identifies contacts who are naturally returning to an active buying phase. This is why even unsegmented email programmes — sometimes called batch-and-blast sending, where the same email is sent to the entire list without segmentation — produce results.

Discovery marketing can be thought of as the complement to targeting. Where targeting delivers content based on what is already known about a contact's behaviour and preferences, discovery marketing involves sending broader content to uncover new areas of interest and to identify contacts who are becoming active again.

Every successful email marketing programme has a combination of active and inactive contacts. The goal is not to remove inactive contacts entirely, but to manage them in a way that captures their value while controlling the deliverability risk they introduce.

How Inactive Contact Data Causes Deliverability Issues

If an established email marketing programme experiences deliverability issues — blocked or bounced emails, or messages going to the junk folder instead of the inbox — the cause is almost always related to the data being sent to.

Email filters operated by mailbox providers (such as Gmail, Microsoft/Outlook, and Yahoo) are designed to deliver emails that recipients find valuable, and to block, suppress, or hide emails that are unwanted. When a sender's domain authentication and email content are consistent and properly configured, a deliverability problem almost always points to the data. In our support case experience, data issues typically fall into one or more of three categories:

  1. Invalid data that should not have been added to the list. This includes mistyped addresses, fake addresses, and bot-generated sign-ups that were not caught by validation at the point of sign-up. For guidance on preventing invalid data from entering a list, see the companion article: Clean Start Validation: How to Prevent Poor-Quality Email Addresses Entering Your List at Sign-Up.
  2. Campaign engagement rate — the ratio of active to inactive contacts in each send. Sending a high volume of email to contacts who do not engage signals to mailbox providers that the content is unwanted, reducing sender reputation over time.
  3. Long-term inactive data that should have been removed. Contacts who have been on the list for an extended period without engaging may include spam traps — email addresses operated by mailbox providers and anti-spam organisations to identify senders with poor list hygiene — and other high-risk addresses that actively damage sender reputation.

When a deliverability issue is suspected, sender authentication and email content should always be tested as part of any investigation. However, in practice, data issues are the most common root cause.

Why Traditional Deliverability Reporting Alone Does Not Prevent Problems

Standard deliverability reporting — covering metrics such as bounce rate, spam complaint rate, domain reputation scores, and inbox placement rate — is diagnostic in nature. It identifies what went wrong and where, but only after the problem has already occurred.

While diagnostic reporting is valuable for understanding past performance and identifying trends, it is inherently reactive. Relying solely on these metrics to guide an email programme leads to a repeating cycle: an issue is detected, a fix is applied, the same or a similar issue recurs, because the underlying cause — typically a data management or targeting problem — has not been addressed.

To break this cycle, email marketers need metrics that monitor the ongoing health and risk factors of the email programme, highlighting where problems are developing before they result in deliverability failures. The following section describes the proactive health metrics I recommend for identifying these risks early.

Proactive Health and Risk Metrics for Email Programmes

I recommend the following metrics for monitoring the health of an email programme proactively. They are designed to highlight risks in data quality, targeting, and list management before those risks cause deliverability problems.

Percentage of Active Compared to Inactive Contacts

What proportion of the mailing list is actively engaging with emails? A declining active percentage over time indicates that list growth is not keeping pace with disengagement, or that re-engagement efforts are insufficient. Monitoring this metric monthly provides an early warning of list health decline.

Monthly Email Volume to Active Compared to Inactive Contacts

How many emails are sent each month to active contacts compared to inactive contacts? This metric reveals how much of the programme's volume is driven by targeted, engagement-based sending compared to broad or untargeted campaigns. A high proportion of volume going to inactive contacts indicates that targeting and automation should be reviewed.

Active Message Volume Percentage

What share of total monthly email volume is sent to active recipients? I recommend a target of 50% or higher, which generally indicates strong list quality and effective targeting. Below this threshold, the programme may be over-relying on inactive contacts to generate volume, which increases deliverability risk.

Inactive Contact Segmentation: Previous Customers Compared to Unengaged Addresses

Among inactive contacts, what proportion are previous customers with a proven purchase or engagement history, compared to contacts who have never meaningfully engaged — sometimes called "zombie" addresses? This distinction matters because previous customers have demonstrated value and may re-engage, while contacts who have never engaged are more likely to be invalid, temporary, or bot-generated. This metric helps assess both list quality and the effectiveness of data lifecycle management.

New Subscriber Engagement Rate

What percentage of new subscribers engage with emails within their first weeks on the list? A low new-subscriber engagement rate may indicate problems with sign-up validation, the effectiveness of the welcome programme, or the quality of the traffic source driving sign-ups. In our experience, approximately 5–10% of new sign-ups remaining completely inactive is a normal baseline. Above 10%, the sign-up process and traffic sources should be investigated.

How to Balance Active and Inactive Contact Management

Managing inactive contacts effectively requires balancing send frequency, content strategy, and re-engagement processes. I recommend the following approaches.

Reduce Send Frequency for Inactive Contacts

Send emails to inactive contacts less often than to active contacts. A practical target is to balance the total monthly email volume so that the number of emails sent to active contacts is equal to or greater than the number sent to inactive contacts.

Most established mailing lists have more inactive contacts than active. This natural imbalance provides a useful frequency guideline. For example, if a mailing list has three times more inactive contacts than active, active contacts should receive approximately three times more emails per month to achieve an even volume balance across the programme.

Use Different Content for Inactive Contacts

Sales-focused content can alienate even loyal customers if they are not in a buying phase, and repeated sales emails to disengaged contacts can train recipients to ignore or filter out future messages. Instead of sales content, email content aligned with blog articles, social media content, educational material, or brand storytelling gives inactive contacts a reason to open, read, and click through to the website — strengthening brand awareness and retention without requiring an immediate purchase.

Introduce Re-Engagement Automation for Returning Contacts

For programmes that use separate content streams for active and inactive contacts, a re-engagement automation sequence — a series of automated emails, similar in structure to a welcome campaign, designed to gradually rebuild engagement — can be introduced for contacts who begin interacting again. This sequence transitions returning contacts back into the main sending programme gradually, rather than immediately placing them back into the full sales email cycle.

How to Recover When Deliverability Issues Occur

If deliverability issues arise — including bounced or blocked emails, or loss of inbox placement — recovery is achievable. The process involves two parallel workstreams: an immediate reputation rebuild using active data, and a longer-term rebalancing of the sending programme to address the underlying cause.

Immediate Steps to Rebuild Sender Reputation

  • Send to active data only. Temporarily restrict sending to new sign-ups and the most engaged contacts. This demonstrates to mailbox providers (such as Gmail, Microsoft/Outlook, and Yahoo) that recipients value the emails, which rebuilds sender reputation and restores inbox placement. In practice, minor issues can recover in a matter of days, while more serious issues may take two to four weeks.
  • Check sign-up processes. Send to new contacts and active contacts in separate campaigns to clearly identify the bounce and engagement rates of new data. New sign-ups should have low bounce rates and high engagement. If they do not, sign-up forms and validation processes should be reviewed to ensure new data is valid and being collected correctly.

Rebalancing the Programme While Reputation Recovers

While the reputation rebuild is underway, use the time to address the underlying causes that led to the issue:

  • Remove the oldest, least-active data. Identify the oldest contacts who have shown no meaningful engagement — particularly those who have been on the list for years without ever clicking a link or visiting the website. This segment is likely to contain spam traps — email addresses operated by mailbox providers and anti-spam organisations to identify senders with poor list hygiene — and other high-risk addresses.
  • Review inactive send frequency. Adjust segments and automation programmes to reduce the weekly and monthly frequency of emails to inactive contacts. When reviewing monthly totals, the target should be for the total volume of emails sent to active contacts to exceed the volume sent to inactive contacts.
  • Review content for inactive contacts. Long-term inactivity is a signal that the content being sent is not what those contacts want. Introduce a different content approach — educational content, brand content, or other material that gives contacts a new reason to open, read, and click through.
  • Restart gradually. Once deliverability has recovered, reintroduce email marketing to inactive contacts with improved data quality, adjusted content strategy, and reduced frequency. Increase volume gradually and monitor the proactive health metrics described in this article to ensure the programme remains balanced.

Summary: Proactive Monitoring and Informed Strategy Work Together

Inactive contacts are a normal and valuable part of every email marketing programme. They generate revenue, support brand awareness, and help identify contacts returning to an active buying phase. However, mismanaging them — through excessive send frequency, irrelevant content, or failure to remove long-term inactive data — is the most common cause of email deliverability problems.

The key principles are:

  • Inactive contacts are normal and should not be excluded entirely. Every successful email programme includes a mix of active and inactive contacts. The goal is to manage the balance, not eliminate one side.
  • Deliverability issues are almost always caused by data problems. Invalid data, poor engagement ratios, and long-term inactive contacts are the most common root causes when authentication and content are already in order.
  • Reactive reporting diagnoses problems but does not prevent them. Traditional deliverability metrics identify issues after they occur. Proactive health metrics — active contact percentage, volume balance, inactive segmentation, and new subscriber engagement — identify risks before they cause failures.
  • Strategy must follow measurement. Health metrics show where the risks are. Strategic actions — validating new data, balancing send frequency, adjusting content for inactive contacts, and managing the data lifecycle — address them.
  • Recovery is possible. When deliverability issues occur, rebuilding sender reputation with active data while rebalancing frequency, content, and data quality resolves the underlying cause and helps prevent recurrence.

Neither measurement nor strategy alone is sufficient. Proactive health monitoring identifies emerging risks; informed data management and targeting decisions address them. Together, they build a sustainable email programme that captures the value of inactive contacts while controlling the deliverability risk they introduce.

entry.title: Re: Recommended process and prerequisites for final WBS/A...
entry.content:
1. Prerequisites to Validate Before Setting WBS to CLSD

Before changing the WBS/AFE to CLSD, validate:

Project System (PS)

WBS status is TECO (or equivalent project completion status).
No open networks, activities, milestones, or subordinate WBS elements.
No open reservations assigned to project activities.
No open project stock.

MM / Procurement

No open PRs.
No open POs.
No pending Goods Receipts (GRs).
No pending Invoice Receipts (IRs).
No remaining commitments.

FI / CO

All actual costs posted.
Period-end settlement executed successfully.
Settlement balances cleared.
AuC capitalization completed (if applicable).
No balance remaining on the WBS.
Budget checks completed (if budget-controlled project).


Recommended Transactions

CJ20N – Project Builder
CJ03 – Display WBS
CJI3 – Actual Cost Line Items
CJI5 – Commitments
S_ALR_87013558 – Cost Elements: Actual/Commitment/Total
CJ88 – Settlement
AIBU/ABJON/AUC reports (depending on asset process)

2. Reports for Key Closure Checks

3. PO Deleted or Fully Consumed but Commitment Appears in CJI5

Before concluding it is a commitment inconsistency, verify:

ME23N

Is PO item really deleted?
Is Final Delivery indicator set?
Is Final Invoice indicator set?

ME2N

Check open quantity/value.

ME5A

Verify whether the originating PR still exists.

CJI5

Review commitment category:
PR commitment
PO commitment
Reservation commitment

Run commitment rebuild/recalculation checks only after confirming source documents are no longer valid.

In many cases, the commitment comes from a remaining PR or partially open purchasing document rather than a true inconsistency.

4. PO Deleted but PR Commitment Remains

This is usually standard behavior if the PR remains active.

Recommended process:

Display PR in ME53N.
Determine whether PR is still required.
If not required:
Delete PR item, or
Set final deletion indicator.
Recheck commitment in CJI5 after update.

Only if:

PR is deleted,
PO is deleted,
and commitment still exists,

should you investigate a potential inconsistency.

entry.title: Configuring Process Parameters in SAP IPD Formulation
entry.content:
Introduction

SAP Integrated Product Development (SAP IPD) represents a transformative shift in how process industry organizations manage product formulations and manufacturing processes. At its core, the IPD framework with among others the Formulation solution provide product developers with a collaborative, integrated platform to manage recipes from initial concept through production. However, one of the more sophisticated features that elevates IPD beyond basic recipe management is the ability to configure and apply process parameters that precisely define how a recipe should be manufactured.

Want to see the full system demo? Check out the recording of our recent Product Expert Training session here (SAP Learning Hub license required).

Process parameters are the manufacturing conditions and constraints that ensure quality and consistency in product production. These parameters can include temperature ranges, processing times, mixing speeds, and pressure requirements - essentially any critical manufacturing condition that must be documented and controlled. This blog provides a comprehensive guide to configuring process parameters in SAP IPD, enabling administrators and product developers to implement production-ready recipe management systems.

Understanding Process Parameters

Process parameters describe the manufacturing conditions under which a recipe should be produced. Rather than simply listing ingredients and their quantities, process parameters allow recipe developers to specify the precise conditions required at each manufacturing stage. In a practical example such as producing apple soda, process parameters might dictate that the pasteurization step requires a specific temperature maintained for a defined duration, followed by mixing at a particular speed for a set time.

These parameters are not optional annotations but essential metadata that ensures regulatory compliance, maintains product quality, and enables effective knowledge transfer between teams and facilities. By embedding process parameters directly within recipe records, organizations create a single source of truth for how products should be manufactured, reducing variability and improving consistency across production sites.

[Image showing the configuration flow as outlined in the text.]

The Three-Step Configuration Framework

Configuring process parameters in SAP IPD follows a clearly defined workflow:

[Image showing steps 1-3 of the configuration flow as outlined in the text.]

Step 1: Property Configuration

The configuration journey begins in the IPD Specification Management’s Properties app, which serves as the template layer for specification attributes. Administrators create a new property specifically designated for Recipe Process Parameters, a special usage classification that signals this property will support manufacturing control parameters.

Within this property, administrators define the specific attributes that every process parameter should inherit. These attributes form the foundation for how process parameters can be used and maintained throughout the system. Common attribute fields include:

  • Value: The primary numeric value of the process parameter
  • Unit of Measure: Specifies whether the parameter is measured in minutes, degrees Celsius, RPM, etc.
  • Minimum and Maximum Values: Define acceptable ranges for the parameter
  • Operators: Allow specification of conditions such as "greater than," "less than," or "equal to"

[Image showing the Properties app with settings for unit of measure and currency]

Architectural insight: A single property configured with these attributes can serve as a template for multiple process parameters. This design principle ensures consistency while eliminating redundant configuration. If product needs evolve and additional attributes are required, administrators can either extend the existing property or create supplementary properties that link to specific process parameters.

Step 2: Data Synchronization

Once the property has been configured in the Properties app, administrators navigate to the Synchronize Data for Formulation" app to synchronize the data. This step ensures that the newly created property definition is propagated to the recipe formulation system, making it available for use when creating actual process parameters.

This explicit synchronization step, though seemingly administrative, serves an important purpose: it creates a clear audit trail and ensures that recipe developers always work with validated, consistent process parameter definitions. Without this synchronization, newly configured properties would remain invisible to the formulation environment.

Step 3: Process Parameter Creation

With data synchronized, administrators proceed to the primary configuration application: IPD Formulation’s Configure Process Parameters. Here, the actual process parameters that will be used in recipes are created and managed.

To create a new process parameter, administrators:

  1. Click on “Create” in the Configure Process Parameter app
  2. Enter the parameter's name and a unique identifier
  3. Optionally add descriptions and translations to support global organizations
  4. Critically, assign the previously configured property to this process parameter

[Image showing the Configure Process Parameters app with properties tab.]

Once the property is assigned, all attributes defined in that property become available in the process parameter automatically. Additionally, administrators can specify default values for minimum and maximum ranges, which will appear as baseline values when recipe developers add this parameter to their recipes.

Finally, administrators must change the process parameter's status from "In Work" to "Released," signaling that the parameter is validated and ready for use in recipe development.

From Configuration to Recipe Application

Once a process parameter reaches "Released" status, product developers gain access to it when creating or editing recipes. The process parameter appears as an available selection in the recipe's Process tab, which is specifically designed for documenting manufacturing stages and their associated conditions.

[Image showing the maintenance of process parameter values as outlined in the text.]

When a recipe developer adds a process parameter to a specific manufacturing stage, such as adding "Mixing Time" to the "Mixing" stage, the system automatically populates all attributes defined in the property. The developer can then:

  • Specify the target value for this manufacturing stage
  • Override default minimum and maximum values if stage-specific conditions differ
  • Select an appropriate unit of measure from the pre-configured options
  • Document any special operational instructions through operator fields

This workflow ensures that process parameters are consistently applied while allowing sufficient flexibility for stage-specific adjustments.

Key Benefits and Design Insights

Scalability and Consistency

The architecture of process parameters in SAP IPD demonstrates excellent scalability. By creating flexible property templates, organizations can define dozens of process parameters while maintaining consistency across all formulations. New parameters can be added without architectural changes or system redesign.

Knowledge Preservation

By formalizing process parameters in system records, organizations preserve institutional knowledge about manufacturing processes. When experienced operators move to different roles or retire, their manufacturing expertise remains documented and accessible to their successors.

Cross-Functional Collaboration

IPD's integration of process parameters with its collaborative environment enables engineering teams, quality assurance, and production teams to align on manufacturing requirements from the outset, reducing miscommunication and revision cycles.

Advanced Configuration Considerations

While the basic workflow is straightforward, administrators should consider several advanced aspects:

  • Allowed Units of Measure: Within property configuration, administrators can restrict the allowed units of measure for a parameter, simplifying user selection and preventing unit conversion errors.
  • Multiple Properties per parameter: While a single property can serve most needs, complex process parameters might require multiple properties. For example, a "Temperature Control" parameter might have one property for steady-state conditions and another for ramp-up specifications.
  • Translation and Localization: The property configuration interface supports multiple languages, enabling organizations with global operations to label parameters appropriately for regional teams.

Conclusion

Configuring process parameters in SAP IPD represents a maturation of recipe management from basic ingredient documentation to comprehensive manufacturing specification. By following the three-step configuration framework - defining property templates, synchronizing data, and creating released parameters - administrators can establish a robust foundation for consistent, auditable, and compliant recipe development.

SAP IPD process parameter functionality exemplifies how modern PLM systems serve not merely as data repositories but as active quality control instruments that embed manufacturing expertise directly into product development workflows.

entry.title: VSR Optimizer Why Its Real Input Isn't Data, It's Judgment
entry.content:
Ask a seasoned dispatcher how they build a day’s plan and you’ll get an answer that sounds like intuition this customer hates early deliveries, that lane always backs up after 3 PM, those two orders ride together because they always have. Ask the SAP TM Vehicle Scheduling and Routing (VSR) optimizer the same question and you get something unsettlingly honest I minimized a number. Tell me what the number should be. The most underappreciated feature in Transportation Management. Not the algorithm, but the question it forces you to answer.

How the VSR Optimizer Works:
The VSR optimizer takes a set of freight units (the demand side) and a set of vehicle resources, schedules and carriers (the supply side). It searches for an assignment: which shipments ride on which vehicles, in what sequence, departing when. The search space is astronomically large. Ten freight units across three trucks already produce more feasible plans than a human can. The optimizer navigates this space against constraints (vehicle capacities, opening hours, driving-time regulations, incompatibilities) and a total cost function, the thing a plan should minimize. Most of the costs in that function are not real.

Understanding Optimization Costs and Penalties:
The cost function blends actual freight charges with penalty costs you invent: a cost per vehicle deployed, a cost per kilometer, a cost per hour, and penalties for early delivery, late delivery and not planning a freight unit at all. None of these invoice anyone. They exist to encode your priorities in a language the algorithm understands.


Figure 1: Planning profile cost settings

Set the non delivery penalty low, and the optimizer will cheerfully leave inconvenient orders behind.
Set earliness and lateness penalties symmetric, and it treats a dock appointment like a suggestion.
Make the per vehicle fixed cost dominant, and it will contort routes to save one truck. This is the part implementation teams underestimate. The optimizer is not a settings screen you configure once; it is a mirror. If your plans come out wrong, the uncomfortable diagnosis is usually that the costs faithfully reflect what you said you value, not what you actually do.

Practical Example:
Freight Consolidation vs Delivery Performance Consider two orders to the same region one 900 kg parcel due Thursday, one 11-tonne load due Friday. A human planner ships them separately: two clean plans, two happy customers, two half-empty trucks. The optimizer, facing a vehicle fixed cost of 500 units against a lateness penalty of 10 per hour, does the arithmetic the planner never writes down. Holding the Thursday order one day and consolidating costs 240 in lateness penalties but saves 500 in vehicle cost. It merges them.

Figure 2: Optimization result with the two Atlanta orders consolidated on one vehicle

Considering Carbon Emissions in Transportation Planning, CO₂ can enter this same calculus. An internal carbon price stops being hypothetical the moment it becomes a cost term the optimizer minimizes alongside distance and duration.

Using VSR Optimization to Improve Transportation Decisions
Run it as a sparring partner, not an autocrat. Interactive planning in the Transportation Cockpit lets planners override the proposal, and the overrides are data. If humans consistently reverse the same category of decision, either train the planners or fix the costs.
Simulate before you commit. Because the cost function is just parameters, counterfactuals are cheap: cut the fleet by two vehicles, tighten delivery windows by four hours, or price carbon at €100 a tonne instead of €50. A profile copy and a re-run replace a consulting engagement.
Let it expose your constraints. Unplanned freight units are the optimizer’s way of filing a complaint. A pattern of unplannable demand on a lane is a procurement insight wearing an error message’s clothing.
Close the loop with execution. Feeding actual transit times back into planning parameters turns every executed freight order into a calibration point.

Conclusion
The SAP TM VSR optimizer demonstrates how transportation planning decisions are influenced not only by freight data and operational constraints but also by the cost parameters and penalties configured by the business. Through the freight consolidation example and practical planning scenarios discussed, we can see how appropriate cost settings, planner judgment, and continuous evaluation of optimization results can improve transportation efficiency and decision making. The key takeaway is that while the optimizer identifies the best solution based on configured objectives, transportation professionals must ensure those objectives reflect actual business priorities.

entry.title: BTP Transports with CTMS & Content Agent | Part 3: Second Content Agent and target in Central
entry.content:
Part 3 of the series BTP Transports with CTMS & Content Agent.

In Part 2 we set up Dev, so a parcel can now be packed and dropped at the source node. In this part we build the receiving end in Central: a second Content Agent that unpacks the parcel, the connection CTMS uses to reach it, and the connection it uses to write into the target Integration Suite.

 

Before you start

The target Integration Suite runs in Central, with the Cloud Integration capability activated (the same rule as in Dev).

Step 1: Process Integration Runtime instance and key

Same as in Dev: an instance of SAP Process Integration Runtime, plan api, with the roles WorkspacePackagesRead, WorkspacePackagesEdit and WorkspacePackagesTransport, and a service key. This time it gives the unpacker access to the target workspace.

Step 2: The second Content Agent

  • Create an instance of Content Agent service with the application plan and the role Import. This is the unpacker.
  • Create a service key. You need its url and, from the uaa section, clientid, clientsecret and url.

Step 3: CloudIntegration destination in Central

The unpacker writes into Integration Suite through a destination named CloudIntegration, filled exactly like the Dev one in Part 2, but from the key of step 1. You can also let the Content Agent UI create it for you when you activate the Cloud Integration content type (see "What tripped me up" first).

Step 4: The transport destination CTMS uses

CTMS needs to know where to deliver the parcel. In Central, create a destination for that. Its name is free; I used CAS_on_target.

FieldValue
URLurl from the Content Agent key (step 2)
AuthenticationOAuth2ClientCredentials
Client ID / secretclientid / clientsecret from the uaa section
Token Service URLurl from the uaa section + /oauth/token

Step 5: Finish the target node

Open CTMS, edit the target node from Part 1 and pick CAS_on_target as its destination. The content type stays Multi-Target Application.

 

The target node with its content type and destination.

A green Check Connection on CAS_on_target only proves the address is reachable (Part 2 explains why). The real test is the first transport in Part 4.

What tripped me up in my setup

  • Three identical runtime instances. Central had three Process Integration Runtime instances with the same name, each in a different Cloud Foundry space, left over from earlier attempts. Before copying a key I had to check which space the target Cloud Integration actually runs in, and use the instance from that space. Clear names would have saved me this.
  • Activating the content type failed because the destination already existed. Activating the Cloud Integration content type in the Content Agent UI creates a CloudIntegration destination for you. I had already created one by hand, so the activation did not go through. entry.title: “Just Take the Exam”: Tammy Powlas’ Journey Through 25 Years of SAP Certification
entry.content:
When Tammy Powlas wanted to attend her first SAP Certification Academy, her boss had a different suggestion: take the exam first. 

It was 2000. Tammy had recently moved into consulting after working on a successful SAP go-live at a large telecommunications company. She had heard good things about the SAP Certification Academy and wanted to attend the Financial Accounting (FI) Academy. 

Instead, her boss encouraged her to go straight for the exam. 

“I think my first boss knew I could pass the exam without attending the Academy,” Tammy recalls. 

He was right. 

Tammy prepared independently by using SAP Help for the FI module. At the time, those learning materials came on CDs. She worked through the material while drawing on what she had already learned through experience. 

Looking back, passing those early Financial Accounting and Controlling exams remains one of the moments she is proudest of. 

“I am proud I took the FI-CO exams by just looking at the SAP Help.” 

That first exam became the beginning of a learning journey that would continue alongside Tammy’s career for the next 25 years. 

Today, learners have more ways to prepare and build their confidence. They can prepare for SAP Certification through free self-paced resources on SAP Learning, with additional guided learning and expert support through SAP Learning Hub.  

When Tammy moved into consulting, certification was valued in the profession. Later, after leaving consulting and moving into a different position, Strategic Enterprise Management became relevant to her work. This time, she attended the SAP Academy in Atlanta. 

Her memory of the experience is succinct: “It was intense.” 

As Tammy’s responsibilities expanded to include SAP Business Warehouse (BW), her learning evolved with them. Earning her BW certification had a particularly important effect. 

“Getting SAP Certified in BW made me confident in my job.” 

That confidence has remained one of the most meaningful parts of certification for Tammy. She never saw it primarily as a way to secure another position. Instead, certification gave her a reason to go deeper into a subject and understand it in a way her everyday work might not otherwise require. 

“Certification forces you to learn the material in a way you haven’t had to before,” she says. 

For Tammy, the result is simple: “It gives me confidence in the areas that I am certified in.” 

As Tammy’s career evolved, so did the areas in which she chose to certify, spanning FI, CO, BW, Strategic Enterprise Management and Accelerated SAP methodology. Each reflected a different area of her professional experience and learning. Some of that learning translated directly into her work. After becoming certified in the Accelerated SAP methodology, Tammy later worked as a project manager and followed the methodology closely throughout a project. The project was a success. 

Today, Tammy is a business analyst as well as an SAP Mentor and ASUG volunteer. She has also watched the experience of learning and becoming certified change considerably since that first exam in 2000. 

One of the biggest changes is practical. 

“Not having to fly to a location, for example, Boston or Atlanta, is a big change in certification,” Tammy says. Proctored exams have changed the experience too. 

Her journey offers a glimpse of just how much can change over the course of a career. Tammy began by studying SAP Help on CDs and travelling to SAP Academies. Twenty-five years later, professionals can access learning and certification in very different ways. 

But the part of her story that matters most has little to do with how the exam is delivered. 

It is about learning something more deeply. It is about challenging what you know. And sometimes, it is about discovering that you are more ready than you think. 

That idea has been there since Tammy’s first certification. Her boss believed she was ready to take the exam without attending the Academy first. Years later, after Tammy earned her most recent certification, the Associate-level SAP Business Warehouse (BW) certification, she received kudos from her boss’s boss. 

For someone considering their first SAP Certification today, Tammy recommends making use of the learning support now available. 

“I recommend joining the SAP Learning Hub, if possible,” she says, pointing to the value of learning with instructors and the certification guidance they can provide. 

Twenty-five years ago, Tammy thought the next step was attending an Academy. Someone else saw that she might already be ready for something bigger. 

So she took the exam. 

For anyone waiting until they feel completely ready to take their own next step, Tammy’s story offers another possibility: perhaps the learning you have already done has prepared you for more than you think. 

And if you are ready to find out what comes next, continue your learning journey with SAP Learning.

entry.title: Re: Non-Mandatory Item Retraining Periods - SF Learning
entry.content:
It's not possible to apply retraining periods to items outside of a curriculum. The Retraining logic (the retraining basis, number, and period fields) of an item is only triggered when that item is part of a curriculum. (2349301 - How to Assign a Retraining Item - LMS - SAP for Me)

It is also recommended to only add items of a required assignment type to a curriculum. If you add an optional assignment type, the user experiences it as required because curriculum assignments remain on users' learning plans indefinitely and has a required date based on the effective date. The only way for a user to clear an optional assignment made by a curriculum is to complete it (either complete it themselves or have a history record added on their behalf). As an alternative to adding optional assignments to a curriculum, you can add an assignment profile that looks for users who completed this learning item and then recommends the optional assignment.
This is outlined further here Creating an Annual Retraining Period Based on a Fixed Date | SAP Help Portal

If you need periodic/recurring training, a curriculum is the only standardmechanism.

entry.title: SAP Focused RUN: Automatically close a guided procedure execution and set a rating
entry.content:
In operations automation, a guided procedure execution sets an overall rating based on the status of steps and activities involved. Sometimes we come across guided procedure executions where an activity for example ‘Check if issue is resolved’ finished successfully without any errors or warning, but other activities involved in the execution ended up in warnings. Considering the critical activity status is success, user should have an option to change the overall rating to success for such executions and prevent any further changes to the execution instance.

To support such a use case, it is now possible to set an overall rating for an execution instance and close the instance. This also ensures that the instance cannot be further modified. We support two approaches in which this feature can be implemented.

Approach 1 : Closure class

In this approach with the help of a custom class implementation we can set an overall rating and further close an instance. If you have a specific use case, for example close an instance if any particular activity resulted in success, then make use of this custom class to implement the logic. Please refer to below steps on how to implement this use case: 

  • Create a Z class that inherits from interface IF_GP_INSTANCE_CLOSURE.
  • Implement method CLOSE_AND_SET_RATING . Please refer below sample code snippet which explains how to retrieve instance context and activity statuses and finally set an overall rating and close the instance.

 

METHOD if_gp_instance_closure~close_and_set_rating.

  DATA:lo_act TYPE REF TO cl_sise_gpf_activity.
   IF it_scope IS NOT INITIAL.
          READ TABLE it_scope ASSIGNING FIELD-SYMBOL(<fs_scope>) INDEX 1.
          IF sy-subrc EQ 0.
            "Fetch instance context for guided procedure instance.This will contain initial cont            ext as well as context data written by activities if any during execution.
                     cl_sise_fwk_db_access=>get_instance_context(
                       EXPORTING
                         iv_instance_guid    =      <fs_scope>-global_id             " Global ID
                       IMPORTING
                         et_instance_context =    DATA(lt_inst_context)              " Instance Context Storage
                     ).

            DATA(lr_instances_object) = cl_sise_scope_factory=>get_instance_by_guid( iv_guid =  <fs_scope>-global_id ).

            IF lr_instances_object IS BOUND.

            DATA(lv_gp_id)   = lr_instances_object->get_gp_id( ).
            DATA(lv_gp_vers) = lr_instances_object->get_gp_version( ).

            DATA(lr_gp) = cl_gpa_access=>get_instance( )->get_gp_by_id(
                  EXPORTING
                    im_id                   = lv_gp_id         " GP ID
                   im_version               = lv_gp_vers " GPA Version
                )-guided_procedure.

                IF lr_gp IS NOT INITIAL.
                  "Fetch gp activities
                DATA(lt_activities) = lr_gp->get_activities( ).
            "Check activity status.
                LOOP AT lt_activities ASSIGNING FIELD-SYMBOL(<fs_act>).
                  lo_act ?= cl_sise_fwk_api=>get_object( iv_object_id =  CONV #( <fs_act>-id )
                                                         iv_object_version = lv_gp_vers
                                                          iv_object_type = cl_sise_fwk_api=>mc_type_activity
                                                          is_scope = <fs_scope> ).
                  IF lo_act IS BOUND.
                  DATA(lv_act_stat) = lo_act->get_status( )->mv_value.
                  ENDIF.
                  ENDLOOP.

              ENDIF.
              " Get scope
              DATA(lmdb_guid) = cl_sise_fwk_util=>get_real_scope_from_scope_obj( is_scope_object = <fs_scope> )-global_id.

            ENDIF.
            "Retrieve gp execution record which needs to be updated
                DATA(ls_ags_gp_run) = cl_sise_fwk_db_access=>get_gp_run_table_record( iv_gp_id = lr_instances_object->get_gp_id( )
                                                                                iv_gp_version = lr_instances_object->get_gp_version( )
                                                                                iv_scope_guid = <fs_scope>-scope_obj->get_global_id( )
                                                                                iv_lmdb_guid  = lmdb_guid
                                                                            ).
                ls_ags_gp_run-closed = 'X'.
                "Set overall rating:S-Success,W-Warning,E-Error
                ls_ags_gp_run-runtime_status = 'S'.
                "Update instance record.This will mark the instance as closed and also overall rating if set will be persisted
                cl_sise_fwk_db_access=>update_gp_run_table( is_record = ls_ags_gp_run ).
          ENDIF.
    ENDIF.

ENDMETHOD

 

  • Next step involves assigning this class to the guided procedure for which executions needs to be closed.
  • Login to your FRUN application and select Operations Automation from FRUN launchpad.
  • Select guided procedure catalog view and edit the guided procedure you wish to implement closure logic.
  • Provide the newly created custom class as below in guided procedure properties

  •  Save and activate guided procedure after closure class is assigned.
  • Create a plan for this guided procedure or execute in background mode. Closure class logic will be executed automatically at last after all activity executions are complete. Based on the closure class implementation the execution instance will be closed and an overall rating will be set.

Note: This approach(closure class implementation) is triggered only during a background guided procedure execution.

Approach 2: Manual closure

User can close a guided procedure execution manually from UI. This is considered another alternative approach to close guided procedure executions. Please refer below steps on how to close executions from UI.

  • Login to your FRUN application and select Operations Automation from FRUN launchpad.
  • In guided procedure instances view, all guided procedure executions are listed..
  • Click on the instance which has to be closed.
  • With the help of 'Close Instance' button , you can close the execution instance.
  • Once you decide to close an instance, a confirmation dialog appears where you have the provision to set an overall rating. This is an optional activity.By default rating field will be pre-filled with current instance rating. If you wish to override this value, you can choose from the available rating options.

  • In case of any errors during closure, an error message will be displayed with details about the error and instance will not be closed.
  • After an instance is closed, it will be locked from any further changes. Hence for closed execution instances below options will not be available anymore.
  1. Perform activity
  2. Adding attachments
  3. Adding comments
  • On successful closure of an instance, it will be marked as closed as in the below snippet.

 

Note: Before closing an execution instance, ensure all activities of the instance are performed. In case there are any activities with status 'Not Performed', closure of such an instance is not supported.

With this feature we provide user the flexibility to extend operations automations and meet their custom requirements.

entry.title: SAP Focused RUN: Pass guided procedure information to an external ticket system
entry.content:
In SAP Focused Run many customers integrate their IT Service Management (ITSM) systems to automatically create tickets when alerts are triggered. In response to these alerts we can execute guided procedures automatically which will help in problem context collection and even activities which helps us to resolve alerts.In this blog we would see how it is possible to pass guided procedure execution details to an external ticket with the help of a BAdI.

Scenario
Customer has connected their ITSM system to SAP Focused Run which enables to create a ticket every time an alert is triggered. Simultaneously, a guided procedure is triggered which is designed to collect problem context or even perform activities without manual intervention. This not only accelerates diagnosis but also lays the groundwork for rapid resolution.

The next step would be updating the ITSM ticket with the results of the Guided Procedure.This improves response times and empowers IT operations with automated workflows.

How to implement this ?

To enable update of tickets with results from a guided procedure in SAP Focused Run, we make use of a Business Add-In (BAdI) that gets triggered during the execution of a guided procedure.

When a Guided Procedure is executed in the background, which is often the case for automated alert reaction flows, BAdI BADI_GP_EXECUTION is triggered during the below lifecycles of the procedure:

  • At the start of the Guided Procedure execution
  • At the end of the Guided Procedure execution
  • At the change of Guided Procedure instance runtime status/closure status

BAdI interface provides below methods:

  • GP_EXECUTION_START       - Triggered during the start of an execution
  • GP_EXECUTION_END           - Triggered during the end of execution
  • GP_EXECUTION_CHANGE   - Triggered whenever the instance runtime/closure  status changes.

Implement the BAdI:

  • Go to transaction SE18
  • Enter the Enhancement Spot as ES_GP_EXECUTION.
  • You will now see BAdI BADI_GP_EXECUTION listed.
  • Create an enhancement implementation Z_ENH_GP_EXECUTION
  • Create a BAdI implementation Z_BADI_GP_EXECUTION, provide an implementation class ZCL_GP_EXECUTION.

Implement methods GP_EXECUTION_START  and GP_EXECUTION_END to retrieve the details you need to pass to the ticket. Sample code snippet below provides an overview on how to retrieve guided procedure execution status or how to fetch guided procedure report details for an execution.

Method- GP_EXECUTION_START

    DATA:lt_exec_stat   TYPE ags_gp_t_exec_status_api,
               lt_messages  TYPE bapiret2_t,
               lv_instance     TYPE char255.

    lv_instance = iv_instance.
    "Fetch GP execution status
    CALL FUNCTION 'FM_GET_GP_EXEC_STATUS'
      EXPORTING
        iv_instance_number  = lv_instance
      IMPORTING
        et_execution_status = lt_exec_stat
        et_messages         = lt_messages.

    READ TABLE lt_exec_stat ASSIGNING FIELD-SYMBOL(<fs_exec_stat>) INDEX 1.
    IF sy-subrc EQ 0.
      DATA(lv_instance_rating) = <fs_exec_stat>-rating.
    ENDIF.
    *Next implement the logic to pass GP execution URL and rating to ticket.

Method-GP_EXECUTION_END

    DATA:lt_exec_stat  TYPE ags_gp_t_exec_status_api,
               lt_messages  TYPE bapiret2_t,
               ls_report         TYPE ags_s_gp_exec_report.

    "Fetch GP execution status
    CALL FUNCTION 'FM_GET_GP_EXEC_STATUS'
      EXPORTING
        iv_instance_number  = iv_instance
      IMPORTING
        et_execution_status = lt_exec_stat
        et_messages               = lt_messages.

    READ TABLE lt_exec_stat ASSIGNING FIELD-SYMBOL(<fs_exec_stat>) INDEX 1.
    IF sy-subrc EQ 0.
      DATA(lv_instance_rating) = <fs_exec_stat>-rating.
    ENDIF.

    "Fetch GP result report
    CALL FUNCTION 'FM_GP_EXEC_REPORT'
      EXPORTING
        iv_instance_id = iv_instance
        iv_rep_type    = 'HTML'
      IMPORTING
        es_report      = ls_report
        et_messages    = lt_messages
      EXCEPTIONS
        rep_failure    = 1
        OTHERS         = 2.
    IF sy-subrc <> 0.
* Implement suitable error handling here
    ENDIF.


 *Next implement the logic to pass GP report and rating to ticket.

Similarly you could have your custom logic built in this badi implementation to fetch the required guided procedure details which needs to be updated in the ticket.

Conclusion

By implementing a BAdI for Guided Procedure execution, you've now extended operations automation to automatically update tickets with actionable context thus closing the loop between alert detection, automated diagnostics, and incident documentation.

This setup brings several key benefits:

  • Reduces manual effort and speeds up resolution time.

  • Improves transparency in ITSM by showing exactly what automation ran.
  • Frees up your operations team to focus on exceptions, not routine tasks.

Quick links

For detailed information on Operations Automation and its capabilities, see Operations Automation expert portal and for more details on Alert Management integration with external systems, see Alert Management -Integration with External Systems

entry.title: SAP Focused RUN Operations Automation: Plugin to display alert data in a guided procedure
entry.content:
In Operations Automation for Alert management, alert reaction guided procedures consists of problem context collection activities and manual activities that guide you through the resolution of an alert.

Alert reaction procedures can be defined for:

  1. System Monitoring alerts
  2. Configuration & Security Analytics alerts
  3. Integration & Cloud Monitoring alerts
  4. Health Monitoring alerts

Let us take up a scenario on how to set up a guided procedure which will be triggered from an Integrating & Monitoring IDoc alert. For problem context collection for the raised alert, we would need an activity in the guided procedure which will help in checking the idoc alerts raised. Let us see the steps involved in setting up such a guided procedure.

1. Plugin and Execution class setup

The foundation of a custom activity lies in two Z-classes: the Plugin Class (for definitions) and the Execution Class (for logic).

a. Create the Z-Plugin Class

First, create a Z-class that inherits from the template plugin class CL_CHECK_COMMON_TPL01_PLG.

  • Attributes: If your plugin needs specific properties, redefine method GET_ATTRIBUTES.

  • Validation: To perform pre-execution checks, redefine method CHECK with your custom validation logic.

  • Activation: Save and activate your class to make it available for GP registration.

b. Create the Z-Execution Class

Next, create a Z-class inheriting from the health check abstraction: CL_GPCR_AP_HEALTH_CHECK_ABS. Redefine method EXECUTE_CONFIGURATION, in our example we will implement a logic to read alert details and identify IDocs in error state. Using this execution class we could also write required parameters to the instance context. Once persisted these values can be

  1. Read by subsequent activities in the same Guided Procedure to decide execution flow.

  2. Retrieved and displayed in the UI for the GP instance.

Code snippet: execute configuration method

data lt_log type ags_sise_tt_log.
data ls_log type line of ags_sise_tt_log.
data lv_status type ags_sise_activity_status.
data lr_exception type ref to cx_root.
data lv_no type n.

"Collect alert details
call method me->get_alert_and_context_details
importing
es_alert = data(lo_alert_object)
rt_metrics_table = data(lt_alerts_metrics_table).

describe table lt_alerts_metrics_table lines data(lv_lines).
if lv_lines > 0.
append lines of lt_alerts_metrics_table to at_table.
me->av_graph_json_data = cl_sise_utility=>convert_table_to_json( iv_table = me->at_table ).
me->av_graph_meta_data = me->build_graph_meta_data( ).
me->save_graph_json_data(
importing
et_log = lt_log
).

lv_no = lv_lines.
clear ls_log.
concatenate lv_no 'IDocs in error status found.'(001) into ls_log-message separated by space..
ls_log-msgty = 'W'.
append ls_log to lt_log.
else.
clear ls_log.
ls_log-message = 'No Idocs in error status found for given alert' .
ls_log-msgty = 'W'.
append ls_log to lt_log.
endif.

else.
clear ls_log.
ls_log-message = 'This activity is valid for ABAP systems only.'(001).
ls_log-msgty = 'W'.
append ls_log to lt_log.
endif.

" save log
save_log_and_status(
it_log = lt_log
iv_status = lv_status
iv_scope_obj = is_obj_guid ).

call method me->write_context.

Code snippet:Writing to instance context

TRY.

CALL METHOD cl_gpcr_alert_helper=>get_gp_alert_map_for_activity
EXPORTING
ir_activity = me
IMPORTING
ev_gpc_alert_map = DATA(ls_alrtgpmap).
ls_context-param_id = 'CONTEXT_ID'.
ls_context-param_descr = 'Alert Context ID'.
ls_context-param_value = ls_alrtgpmap-context_id .
APPEND ls_context TO lT_CONTEXT.
ls_context-param_id = 'ALERT_TYPE_ID'.
ls_context-param_descr = 'Alert Type ID'.
ls_context-param_value = ls_alrtgpmap-alert_type_id.
APPEND ls_context TO lT_CONTEXT.
ls_context-param_id = 'HASHMETRICPATH'.
ls_context-param_value = ls_alrtgpmap-hash_metric_path.
APPEND ls_context TO lT_CONTEXT.
ls_context-param_id = 'START_DATE_UTC'.
ls_context-param_value = ls_alrtgpmap-start_date_utc.
APPEND ls_context TO lT_CONTEXT.
ls_context-param_id = 'START_TIME_UTC'.
ls_context-param_value = ls_alrtgpmap-start_time_utc.
APPEND ls_context TO lT_CONTEXT.
me->set_instance_context( it_act_param_ctxt = lt_CONTEXT ).
CATCH cx_sise_exception. " Composition Exception Class
ENDTRY.

2. Guided Procedure Maintenance

Once your classes are active, you must map them to a Guided Procedure. So create a guided procedure against relevant application area, in our example it would be 'Integration Monitoring'.

  • Create Automatic Activity: Create a new Plugin Activity.

  • Registration: Enter the names of the Z-Plugin and Z-Execution classes created earlier.

  • Maintain Plugin attributes: Set plugin attribute defined in the plugin class.

  • Search Attributes: To ensure the GP triggers correctly from an alert:

    • Navigate to Properties > Search Attributes.

    • Maintain the Alert Name.

    • Check the flag for Automatic Execution if needed.

  • Save and Activate: Once all your setup is done, check for any errors and then activate guided procedure.

Note on Transporting: When moving a guided procedure across landscapes, only the plugin/activity definitions are included in the guided procedure transport. You must transport your Z-classes in a separate TR to ensure functionality in the target system

For a deep dive into the configuration of the Alert Management (AEM) side on how to map specific alerts to your new guided procedure, refer to the official SAP Expert Portal guide:

Alert reaction process

3. Monitoring: Viewing the Instance Context

To verify that your context values (like CONTEXT_ID or HASHMETRICPATH ) are being captured during runtime:

  1. Open the Guided Procedure Execution Instance.

  2. Navigate to the Step List.

  3. Click the Display Context Data button.

Here, you will see a combined view of the initial context and the dynamic values written by your execution class.

Conclusion

By combining custom execution classes with instance context persistence, you can create highly automated workflows in SAP Focused Run. Whether it is identifying IDoc errors or passing system metrics between steps, the flexibility of the plugin architecture allows for robust system management.

Next Steps: If you are interested in how to set up automatic/manual activities that capture user input into the instance context, check out our follow-up blog .

entry.title: SAP Focused RUN Operations Automation: Capture user inputs from automatic or manual activities
entry.content:
In SAP Focused RUN Operations Automation, both automatic and manual activities support predefined inputs, similar to a questionnaire attached to each activity.

For automatic activities, the runtime execution class can be enhanced to deliver the required inputs programatically. For manual  activities, these inputs are set up at design time when designing the guided procedure. During guided procedure execution, users can provide answer to these inputs. The responses are captured and stored in the guided procedure context, making them available across guided procedure instance.

Defining inputs for automatic activity

To explain how to set up inputs for activities, let us consider a guided procedure that retrieves IDocs in error.

Step 1 : Change the Activity Type to "Automatic with Input"

For automatic activities that require inputs, change the activity type to Automatic with Input

METHOD get_type.
 re_type = 'F'.
ENDMETHOD.

Step 2 : Capture IDoc error details to the Guided Procedure Context

Before defining input fields, capture all required IDoc error details into the guided procedure context so they can be retrieved later. The following sample code from the EXECUTE_CONFIGURATION method retrieves IDocs in error and saves them to the instance context:

 
   METHOD execute_configuration.

   DATA lt_log       TYPE ags_sise_tt_log.
   DATA ls_log       TYPE LINE OF ags_sise_tt_log.
   DATA lv_status    TYPE ags_sise_activity_status.
   DATA lr_exception TYPE REF TO cx_root.
   DATA lv_no TYPE n.

 TRY.
   IF cl_system_check_assist=>is_abap_system_check( is_obj_guid = is_obj_guid ) EQ abap_true.

     "Collect IDocs for alert
     CALL METHOD me->get_alert_and_context_details
       IMPORTING
         es_alert         = DATA(lo_alert_object)
         rt_metrics_table = DATA(lt_alerts_metrics_table).
         
     "aggregate IDoc list by idoc type, status
     CALL METHOD me->aggregate_alert_details
       EXPORTING
         it_metrics_table     = lt_alerts_metrics_table
       IMPORTING
         rt_metrics_table_agg = DATA(lt_idoc_table_agg).


     DESCRIBE TABLE lt_idoc_table_agg LINES DATA(lv_lines).
     IF lv_lines > 0.

       "display aggregated IDoc lsit in UI
       APPEND LINES OF lt_idoc_table_agg TO  at_table.
       me->av_graph_json_data = cl_sise_utility=>convert_table_to_json( iv_table = me->at_table ).
       me->av_graph_meta_data = me->build_graph_meta_data( ).
       me->save_graph_json_data(
       IMPORTING
       et_log   = lt_log
       ).

  ELSE.
       CLEAR ls_log.
       ls_log-message = 'No Idocs in error status found for given alert' .
       ls_log-msgty = 'W'.
       APPEND ls_log TO lt_log.
     ENDIF.

   ELSE.
     CLEAR ls_log.
     ls_log-message = 'This activity is valid for ABAP systems only.'(001).
     ls_log-msgty = 'W'.
     APPEND ls_log TO lt_log.
   ENDIF.

   " save log
   save_log_and_status(
     it_log       = lt_log
     iv_status    = lv_status
     iv_scope_obj = is_obj_guid ).
  
  " Write idocs data to context

   CALL METHOD me->write_context.

CATCH cx_sise_model cx_sise_log cx_sise_exception INTO lr_exception.

ENDTRY.

ENDMETHOD.

Step 3: Define Inputs Programmatically

Retrieve the IDoc details from the context and define the input fields by redefining the GET_MANUAL_INPUTS method in the runtime execution class:

 
METHOD get_manual_inputs.
    DATA: lt_context TYPE ags_sise_t_inst_context.
    DATA:ls_manual_input TYPE ts_manual_inp.
    DATA lv_idoctp TYPE string.
    DATA lv_status TYPE string.
    DATA lv_msg TYPE string.
    DATA lv_number TYPE string.
    DATA lv_dummy TYPE string.
    CALL METHOD me->get_instance_context
      EXPORTING
        iv_snapshot     = 'X'
      IMPORTING
        et_inst_context = lt_context.

    LOOP AT lt_context INTO DATA(ls_context) WHERE param_id = 'IDOCS' .
      SPLIT ls_context-extra_key AT space INTO: lv_number lv_idoctp lv_status lv_msg.

      SHIFT lv_msg LEFT DELETING LEADING space.
      SPLIT lv_msg  AT space INTO: lv_dummy lv_msg.

      ls_manual_input-input_id = 'INPUTPROC' .
      ls_manual_input-input_extra_key = ls_context-extra_key .
      CONCATENATE 'How to process IDocs with error " ' lv_msg '" ?'  INTO  ls_manual_input-INPUT_text SEPARATED BY space.
      ls_manual_input-input_text_desc = 'Choose what to do with the IDocs'.
      ls_manual_input-input_type = 'D'. "Drop down'.
      ls_manual_input-input_value_hlp = 'MAIL:Send Notification Mail ,REPROCESS:Reprocess,IGNORE:Ignore'.
      APPEND ls_manual_input TO et_manual_inp.

    ENDLOOP.

  ENDMETHOD.

Supported Input Field Types

The following input field types are currently supported:

 
Type Code Description
Multi-value dropdownMAllows multiple selections
Single-select dropdownDAllows one selection
Text fieldTFree-text entry
CheckboxCBoolean toggle

Below are sample code snippets for each type:

 
ls_manual_input-input_id = 'INP_MULTI'.
   ls_manual_input-input_type = 'M'. "Multi Value
   ls_manual_input-input_text = 'Select supported languages'.
   ls_manual_input-input_text_desc = ''.  "Pass the text which should be available as tooltip
   ls_manual_input-input_value_hlp = 'EN:English,FR:French,DE:German'. "Format to be followed is KEY1:VALUE1,KEY2:VALUE2...
   APPEND ls_manual_input TO et_manual_inp.

   ls_manual_input-input_id = 'INP_DRP'.
   ls_manual_input-input_type = 'D'. "Drop down
   ls_manual_input-input_text = 'Are you able to navigate to the link provided'.
   ls_manual_input-input_text_desc = ''. "Pass the text which should be available as tooltip
   ls_manual_input-input_value_hlp = 'Y:Yes,N:No'.  "Format to be followed is KEY1:VALUE1,KEY2:VALUE2...
   ls_manual_input-is_mandatory = 'X'.
   APPEND ls_manual_input TO et_manual_inp.

   ls_manual_input-input_id = 'INP_TEXT'.
   ls_manual_input-input_type = 'T'. "Text
   ls_manual_input-input_text = 'No:of long running jobs'.
   ls_manual_input-input_text_desc = ''. "Pass the text which should be available as tooltip
   APPEND ls_manual_input TO et_manual_inp.

   ls_manual_input-input_id = 'INP_CB'.
   ls_manual_input-input_type = 'C'. "Check Box
   ls_manual_input-input_text = 'Text Execution'.
   APPEND ls_manual_input TO et_manual_inp.

Step 4 : Activate and Execute the Guided Procedure

Activate the runtime execution class and execute the guided procedure. Any activities waiting for user input will be highlighted in the Guided Procedure Instances UI. Once the user provides and saves their inputs, the highlighting is removed.

Step 5: View the Dynamically Loaded Inputs

Click on the instance to open the activity waiting for user input. Since this is an automatic activity, the runtime execution class is triggered in the background and retrieves the inputs defined programmatically.

Step 6: Save Inputs to Guided Procedure Context

The final step is for the user to select or provide an input and click Save. This saves the inputs to the guided procedure context and changes the activity status to Success. Click the Context button to view the saved inputs

Defining inputs for manual activity

Using the same guided procedure example, let us look at how inputs can be defined for a manual activity. Unlike automatic activities, inputs for manual activities are defined at design time within the guided procedure authoring UI.

Step 1: Define Inputs at Design Time and Activate the Guided Procedure

When adding or editing a manual activity in the guided procedure authoring UI:

  1. Set the Input option to Simple
  2. Click Add to insert a new input row
  3. Fill in the fields according to the type of input required

Note: For multi-value dropdown or single-select dropdown inputs, click the Drop Down Items button to add the values to be displayed.

Once all required inputs are added, save and activate the guided procedure.

Step 2: Execute the Guided Procedure

When the guided procedure is executed, the defined inputs are displayed within the manual activity. Similar to automatic activities, provide the required inputs and click Save. The inputs are saved to the guided procedure context and remain available for the instance.

Note: During background execution of a guided procedure, if the execution reaches an activity that is awaiting inputs, all subsequent automatic activity executions are paused. Once inputs have been provided and saved for the manual or automatic activity, click the Execute Activities in Background button to resume execution of all following automatic activities.

 

Conclusion

Activity inputs in SAP Focused RUN Operations Automation bring a powerful layer of flexibility to guided procedures. Whether you are working with automatic activities or manual activities, the framework provides a consistent and intuitive way to capture user responses during execution.

By storing these inputs in the guided procedure context, they remain accessible throughout the guided procedure instance, enabling downstream activities to act on the information provided.

Next Steps: If you are interested in how to enable/disable steps or activities in a guided procedure using condition approach, you can refer this blog

entry.title: SAP Focused RUN Operations Automation: Controlling visibility and execution of steps and activities
entry.content:
In SAP Focused RUN Operations Automation, guided procedures are designed to streamline operational workflows. However, not every step or activity is relevant in every situation. To address this, we have introduced Execute Conditions, a feature that controls the visibility and executability of steps and activities based on predefined conditions.

Execute Conditions allow you to define a criteria that must be met before a step or activity becomes visible and executable  during guided procedure execution. If the condition is not satisfied, the step or activity is simply skipped, keeping the guided procedure clean and focused on what is relevant for the current situation.

Defining Execute Conditions at Design Time

In the guided procedure authoring UI, the Execute Condition section is available as part of both step and activity properties. Three options are provided:

 
Always (default)The step or activity is always visible and executable
Based on statusThe step or activity is visible only if a previous step or activity has a specific status
Based on context valueThe step or activity is visible only if a specific value exists in the guided procedure instance context

 

Controlling Activity Visibility Based on User Input

To understand this better, let us revisit the guided procedure that retrieves IDoc errors, already explored in blog  where users provide inputs that are stored in the guided procedure context.

The Scenario

In the first step of this guided procedure contains an activity that retrieves all IDoc errors and asks the user how to process them. Based on the user's selection, the following activities should be shown or hidden:

  • If the user selects Reprocess → enable the Reprocess IDoc activity and hide the Notify Responsible Persons activity
  • If the user selects Mail → enable the Notify Responsible Persons activity and hide the Reprocess IDoc activity

This conditional behavior can be achieved using the context values saved when the user submits their input.

Step 1: Define the Execute Condition at Design Time

While designing the guided procedure, maintain the execute condition for each activity based on the corresponding context value. During execution, the guided procedure reads the context values and evaluates whether the condition is satisfied.

Step 2: User Provides Input During Execution

When the guided procedure runs, the user provides an input to the first activity specifying how to handle the IDoc error. This input is saved to the guided procedure context as shown below.

Step 3: Execute Condition Is Evaluated

With the input saved to context, the execute condition defined for the following activity is evaluated. Since the condition is now satisfied, the corresponding activity in this case 'Notify Responsible Persons'  becomes visible and executable, while the other activity remains hidden.

Note: The walkthrough above demonstrates execute conditions applied at the activity level using a context value condition. A similar result can also be achieved using the status condition, where the visibility of a activity is controlled based on the status of a previous activity. The same concept applies equally to step conditions when a condition is defined at the step level, the entire step and all its activities are shown or hidden based on the defined criteria, following the same evaluation logic described above.

Conclusion

Execute Conditions make guided procedures smarter and more adaptive. By linking step and activity visibility to runtime context values or previous activity or step statuses, you can build guided procedures that dynamically adjust to the situation at hand , ensuring users are presented with only the actions that are relevant to their specific scenario.

entry.content:
Verify whether the value populated in the PR Agreement field is actually a Purchase Order instead of a Contract or Scheduling Agreement.

 Step 1: Identify the Agreement Number in the PR

  1. Open the affected Purchase Requisition in ME53N.
  2. Navigate to the Source of Supply tab.
  3. Note the value in the Agreement field.

 

Step 2: Verify the Document Type

  1. Execute transaction SE16H.
  2. Enter table EKKO.
  3. Enter the Agreement number from the PR in field EBELN.
  4. Execute the query.

Review field BSTYP:

BSTYP

Meaning

F

Purchase Order

K

Contract

L

Scheduling Agreement

 

Step 3: Analyze the Result

Expected Behavior

  • Agreement field should contain:
    • Contract (BSTYP = K), or
    • Scheduling Agreement (BSTYP = L)

Abnormal Behavior

  • If the document found has:

BSTYP = F

then a Purchase Order is being stored in the Agreement field, which is not standard SAP behavior.

 

Step 4: Investigate Source Determination

If a PO is found in the Agreement field, review the following:

  1. ME03 – Source List
    • Check fixed source of supply.
    • Check agreement references.
  2. ME13 – Purchasing Info Record
    • Verify source and vendor assignment.
  3. MEQ3 – Quota Arrangement
    • Verify whether MRP selected the source via quota arrangement.
  4. Custom Enhancements:
    • BAdI MD_PURREQ_CHANGE
    • BAdI MD_MODIFY_SOURCE
    • BAdI ME_PROCESS_REQ_CUST
    • Any Z-enhancements executed during MRP run.

 

Conclusion

If the value in EBAN-KONNR (Agreement) points to an EKKO record with BSTYP = F (Purchase Order), the issue is likely caused by:

  • Incorrect source determination master data, or
  • Custom enhancement logic populating the Agreement field during PR creation.

This is not standard expected SAP behavior and should be investigated further.

entry.title: Personnel Calculation Rule - Factoring Parameter
entry.content:
Introduction

Accurate payroll execution is the backbone of employee life cycle management, and ensuring employees are compensated precisely for days worked—while factoring in complex absence structures—is a critical daily challenge for SAP consultants. In this blog post, we will walk through a practical Personnel Calculation Rule (PCR) that bridges Time Management and Payroll by leveraging variables like TKSOLL and TKAP to determine exact calendar days worked and streamline wage type valuation.

Importance of PCR:

In an employee life cycle payroll plays a major role. Generally an employee gets paid for the number of days worked in a particular payroll period/cycle. Payroll calculations takes place based company policy. Here let's take a scenario where they excludes paid absence and finds exact calendar days an employee worked in a particular period

Operations used:

TKSOLL - Takes planned working time in Calendar days.

TKAP** - Paid absence in Calendar days.

PCR Syntax:

*

XXXX

RTE=TKSOLL       * Sets rate to planned calendar days

RTE-TKAP**       * Subtracts unpaid absences

ADDWT *          * Adds wage type to output table

PCR Image:

Explanation:

  • In the above sample PCR we initially check for the wagetype which needs to be processed.
  • Then we set Rate equals to TKSOLL, which means the rate is equal to number of calendar days in planned working time. This varies from employee to employee based on the work schedule which is assigned to them. The work schedule determines the working time/shift of an employee with breaks, public holidays configured in it.
  • Then the rate is being subtracted by the paid absence with counting class 06 followed by paid absence with counting class 07 and 09.
  • Finally stores the calculated Rate in the wage type which is being processed.

Conclusion:

Mastering payroll factoring through custom PCRs gives you the flexibility to meet organizational policies by utilizing TKSOLL for planned calendar days and subtracting paid absences via TKAP to reflect true working times. Implementing this approach improves accuracy and transparency across your payroll and time management modules, so feel free to share your thoughts, questions, or alternative approaches in the comments below.
